title: The Bowge of Courte
description: Skelton's first major poem, a dream satire in rhyme royal: the dreamer Drede boards the ship Bowge of Courte, where the personified vices of the court — Flattery, Suspicion, Harvy Hafter, Disdain, Riot, Deceit — successively menace and betray him, until he leaps overboard. It is the founding text of the Tudor court-satire tradition.
plot_or_argument: Drede, standing at the shore, is invited aboard the Bowge of Courte; each passenger woos him and then turns on him, and the poem breaks off as he prepares to leap from the ship to save his life.
narrative_structure: Dream vision with prologue; an allegorical sea voyage in which successive encounters with the courtly vices build to a single climactic decision to abandon the court.
principal_characters: Drede (the dreamer); Flattery; Suspicion; Harvy Hafter; Disdain; Riot; Deceit
meter_and_prosody: Seven-line rhyme royal stanzas, handled with Chaucerian fluency but a distinctly satirical edge.
historical_context: Written at the turn of the century, when Skelton was moving from court service to the country living at Diss; its portrait of court corruption anticipates his later anti-Wolsey satires.
literary_significance: The first sustained court satire of the English Renaissance, combining the dream vision of Chaucer with the estates satire of the Middle Ages and setting the pattern for the complaint literature of the sixteenth century.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1499.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Wynkyn de Worde, c. 1499. Standard edition: John Scattergood (ed.), John Skelton: The Complete English Poems (Penguin, 1983).

title: Philip Sparrow
description: A mock-elegy of some 1,400 Skeltonic lines in which Jane Scrope, a young gentlewoman of the household at Carrow Abbey, laments her pet sparrow Philip, killed by the cat Gib — the lament swelling into a virtuoso parody of the Latin Office of the Dead, with a commendation of Jane and a digressive defense of women.
plot_or_argument: Jane Scrope mourns her sparrow; the poem moves from tender elegy through liturgical parody (Placebo, Dirige) to the praise of Jane's beauty and virtue, ending with an envoy sending the book to her.
narrative_structure: A single-voiced lament that repeatedly breaks its frame: elegy, liturgical parody, blazon, and envoy succeed one another by association.
principal_characters: Jane Scrope; Philip (the sparrow); Gib (the cat)
meter_and_prosody: The Skeltonic at its most supple: short lines of two or three stresses, tumbling rhymes, and Latin tags woven into English.
historical_context: Written for the household of Sir Philip Calthorpe's widow at Carrow; the text's allusions to Jane Scrope's family place it about 1505.
literary_significance: The classic of the English mock-elegy and a touchstone of Skelton's art; its play with the liturgy and its defense of women made it one of the most read poems of the century.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Kele, c. 1545 (earlier editions c. 1508). Standard edition: Scattergood (1983).

title: The Tunning of Elinour Rumming
description: Skelton's carnivalesque masterpiece: a Skeltonic account of the alewife Elinour Rumming of Leatherhead and the procession of women who come to drink her noxious ale, a low-life gallery from drunken Alice to the beggarly Maud Ruggy — ugliness, appetite, and disorder rendered with gleeful verbal energy.
plot_or_argument: The poem describes Elinour's brewing and her customers in turn — their poverty, their lechery, their brawling — as the alehouse degenerates into a riot of appetite without plot or moral.
narrative_structure: A catalogue or procession of drinkers, framed by the description of the brewing; no plot, but a mounting carnival intensity.
principal_characters: Elinour Rumming; her customers (drunken Alice, Maud Ruggy, and others)
meter_and_prosody: The Skeltonic at its most anarchic — breathless rhymes, macaronic puns, and tavern speech.
historical_context: Set at Leatherhead in Surrey; the poem belongs to the alehouse satire of the early sixteenth century and reflects the moralists' anxieties about disorderly women.
literary_significance: The most vivid low-life poem in English before the eighteenth century; its catalogue form and demotic energy made it a model for later satire.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1521. Standard edition: Scattergood (1983).

title: Magnificence
description: Skelton's morality play: Prince Magnificence, a figure of the good ruler (and transparently of Henry VIII), is seduced by the courtly vices — Fansy, Counterfeit Countenance, Cloaked Collusion, Courtly Abusion — into riot and misrule, stripped of his wealth and driven to despair, and finally restored by Good Hope, Perseverance, and Measure.
plot_or_argument: Liberty and Measure advise the Prince against Fansy; Magnificence follows the vices, is robbed and reduced to suicidal despair by Adversity, and is rescued by Good Hope, Redress, and Perseverance, who restore him to the rule of Measure.
narrative_structure: A full-scale morality in the tradition of Everyman, with a political allegory of the prince's fall and amendment; the Vice roles carry the comic weight.
principal_characters: Magnificence; Fansy; Counterfeit Countenance; Cloaked Collusion; Courtly Abusion; Adversity; Good Hope; Perseverance; Measure
meter_and_prosody: Couplets and short stanzas of functional verse, with Skeltonic flourishes in the Vice speeches.
historical_context: Written in the years of Wolsey's ascendancy, when Skelton watched the young king's government with alarm; the play reads as a warning to Henry VIII against misrule and extravagance.
literary_significance: The first English morality play with a political programme and the bridge between the medieval moralities and the Tudor interludes; it established the genre of the king-as-everyman that Bale and the Elizabethans inherited.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1530 (the only early edition). Standard edition: Scattergood (1983); modern edition: Paula Neuss (ed.), Magnificence (Manchester University Press, 1980).

title: Speke Parrot
description: The first of Skelton's great anti-Wolsey satires: a parrot — polyglot, learned, and fearless — speaks the court's dangerous truths in a torrent of macaronic verse, attacking the Cardinal's pride, his monopoly of the king's ear, and the corruption of the church, all under the parrot's traditional licence of the fool.
plot_or_argument: The Parrot complains of his cage and his mistress's neglect, then turns to the abuses of the age: Wolsey's supremacy, clerical greed, and the decay of learning; the poem closes with a prayer for amendment.
narrative_structure: A monologue of the speaking bird in the complaint tradition, shifting between personal grievance and public satire without fixed argument.
principal_characters: the Parrot; (implicitly) Cardinal Wolsey
literary_form: verse satire in Skeltonics with macaronic Latin
meter_and_prosody: Skeltonic lines studded with Latin, Greek, and school tags; the parrot's 'speaking' is a display of learned polyglot wit.
historical_context: Written in 1521 as Wolsey's power peaked; the parrot's cage is the poet's own position under surveillance, and the poem circulates the satirical truths the court could not speak.
literary_significance: The founding text of the English tradition of political satire under censorship; its speaking-bird device recurs through the century to Spenser and beyond.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1545 by Richard Kele (with Philip Sparrow and Colin Clout). Standard edition: Scattergood (1983).

title: Colin Clout
description: Skelton's longest satire: the plain countryman Colin Clout — a persona borrowed from the shepherd-poets, which Spenser later took up — reports what the commons say of the clergy: their pomp, their ignorance, their neglect of preaching, and the corruption of the bishops, all in the voice of 'the people's' plain truth.
plot_or_argument: Colin sets out to speak 'of the spiritual estate'; the poem catalogues the clergy's abuses through the reported speech of the commons, answers the expected objections of the bishops, and ends with an appeal to the lay powers for reform.
narrative_structure: A long single-voiced complaint organized as report ('the commons say...') with interposed answers to clerical objections; the plain man's persona licenses the satire.
principal_characters: Colin Clout; the clergy (collectively)
meter_and_prosody: Sustained Skeltonics over 1,200 lines; the metre's repetitiveness enacts the commons' insistent complaint.
historical_context: Written as the Reformation crisis gathered, about 1522; the poem voices the anticlericalism of the laity without committing itself to the Lutheran programme.
literary_significance: The great English anticlerical satire of its age and the direct ancestor of Spenser's Colin Clout; its plain-man persona became a convention of English satire.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1531 by William de Worde. Standard edition: Scattergood (1983).

title: Why Come Ye Nat to Courte?
description: Skelton's most direct assault on Cardinal Wolsey: taking up the courtiers' question of the title, the poet answers that the court is barred to all but Wolsey's creatures, and proceeds to a full-scale attack on the Cardinal's arrogance, his building, his rule of the king, and the degradation of the realm under his hand.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the question of why honest men shun the court, answers that Wolsey has shut the king away from his subjects, and develops into a sustained invective against the Cardinal's person and policy, closing with a warning to the king.
narrative_structure: A satirical diatribe organized as an answer to a question; cumulative invective rising to direct warning.
principal_characters: the poet (speaker); Cardinal Wolsey
meter_and_prosody: Skeltonics of unusual venom and speed; the metre's rattle becomes a weapon.
historical_context: Written when Wolsey's power was absolute and Skelton had taken sanctuary at Westminster (1523) to escape the Cardinal's anger; the poem circulated in manuscript before printing.
literary_significance: The most fearless political satire of the early Tudor period and the classic of the English anti-court diatribe.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1545 by Richard Kele. Standard edition: Scattergood (1983).

title: The Garland of Laurel
description: Skelton's self-crowning dream vision: the poet, wandering in a forest, is brought before Queen Fame and the assembled court of the Countess of Surrey at Sheriff Hutton, where Pallas and the ladies of the court intercede for him and Fame grants him the laurel — the poem including a catalogue of his own works that is the first English poet's bibliography.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer debates with Occupation and Fame whether he deserves the laurel; the ladies of the court, led by the Countess of Surrey, petition on his behalf; Fame crowns him, and the poet wakes to compose the envoy of praise.
narrative_structure: Dream vision with debate and pageant; the catalogue of the poet's works embedded in the intercession of the court ladies.
principal_characters: the poet; Queen Fame; Pallas; the Countess of Surrey; Occupation
literary_form: dream vision in rhyme royal and Skeltonics
meter_and_prosody: Mixed rhyme royal and Skeltonic passages; the courtly and the demotic styles deliberately alternated.
historical_context: Written at Sheriff Hutton in Yorkshire, in the household of the Countess of Surrey, in 1523, when Skelton's laureate claims needed the court's support against Wolsey.
literary_significance: The first English poem to canonize its own author, with a bibliography of his works; a unique document of the poet's self-understanding at the Tudor court.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Fakes, 1523. Standard edition: Scattergood (1983).

title: Wyatt's Poems
alternative_titles: Sonnets and Lyrics of Sir Thomas Wyatt
description: The collected shorter poems of Sir Thomas Wyatt — sonnets translated and imitated from Petrarch, rondeaux, epigrams, and songs — including the masterpieces 'Whoso list to hunt', 'They flee from me', 'My galley charged with forgetfulness', and 'Blame not my lute'. They circulated in court manuscript during his life; ninety-six were printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
plot_or_argument: A lyric sequence without narrative frame: the poems trace the courtly lover's service, betrayal, and disenchantment, and the courtier's peril under the prince's eye.
narrative_structure: Manuscript miscellany; the Egerton MS (with Wyatt's own revisions) is the principal witness, supplemented by Tottel's printed text.
principal_characters: the speaker; the beloved (variously identified); the court
meter_and_prosody: The first English sonnets, in deliberately rough iambic pentameter with enjambment against rhyme; songs in short lines built for music.
historical_context: Written across Wyatt's diplomatic career and his two imprisonments (1536, 1541); the poems encode the dangers of Henrician court life in the idiom of Petrarchan love.
literary_significance: The foundation of the English lyric: Wyatt brought the Petrarchan sonnet and the courtly song into English, and his 'difficult' style set the standard of authenticity the Elizabethans imitated.
attribution_notes: The canon rests on the Egerton MS and Tottel; a few poems printed under Wyatt's name in 1557 are of uncertain authorship.
bibliographical_notes: Egerton MS 2711 (British Library); Tottel's Miscellany (1557). Standard edition: R. A. Rebholz (ed.), Sir Thomas Wyatt: The Complete Poems (Penguin, 1978).

title: The Penitential Psalms
description: Wyatt's paraphrase of the seven penitential psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143), framed by a prologue in which David, the royal lover of Bathsheba, is made the type of the penitent courtier. Based on Aretino's I Sette Salmi, the work turns the psalmist's repentance into a sustained meditation on the dangers of the court and the sovereignty of God.
plot_or_argument: The frame narrative follows David from his sin with Bathsheba through the prophet Nathan's parable to his repentance; each psalm is then paraphrased as David's own speech, with Wyatt's added commentary.
narrative_structure: Prologue narrative (in terza rima) followed by seven paraphrases; each psalm introduced by a stanza of commentary.
principal_characters: David; Bathsheba; Nathan
literary_form: psalm paraphrase in terza rima (prologue) and various stanzas
meter_and_prosody: Terza rima in the prologue — the first sustained English use of Dante's metre — and ottava rima in the psalm paraphrases.
historical_context: Written after Wyatt's imprisonment of 1536, during the fall of Anne Boleyn; the psalmist's court becomes a mirror of Henry VIII's, and repentance the courtier's only safety.
literary_significance: The major English religious poem of the Reformation's first generation and the ancestor of Sidney's and Milton's psalm paraphrases; its David is the first great self-portrait of the Tudor courtier in verse.
bibliographical_notes: Printed 1549 (Thomas Petyt?). Standard edition: Rebholz (1978).

title: Wyatt's Satires
description: Three verse epistles — 'Mine own John Poins', 'My mother's maids', and 'A spending hand' — written from Wyatt's Kentish retirement after his 1536 imprisonment: adaptations of Horace and Alamanni in which the speaker rejects the court's falseness and the town's corruption for the honest poverty of the country life.
plot_or_argument: Each epistle weighs the court against the country: to Poins, the speaker explains why he cannot flatter; to the courtiers, why he will not hunt with them into the wind; to Bryan, why honesty is the only policy he can keep.
narrative_structure: Three independent verse epistles in the Horatian manner, linked by their common theme of withdrawal from the court.
principal_characters: the speaker; John Poins; Francis Bryan
meter_and_prosody: Terza rima throughout — the metre of the Penitential Psalms prologue — giving the epistles a grave, conversational movement.
historical_context: Written at Allington after Wyatt's release from the Tower in 1536; the satires voice the disillusion of the courtier who has survived the fall of Anne Boleyn.
literary_significance: The first English satires in the classical manner and the models for the Elizabethan verse epistle and satire (Donne, Hall, Marston); their country-house ideal anticipates the seventeenth-century poems of retirement.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in Tottel's Miscellany (1557). Standard edition: Rebholz (1978).

title: Surrey's Poems
alternative_titles: Sonnets and Lyrics of Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
description: The collected shorter poems of the Earl of Surrey — sonnets in the new 'English' form he devised (three quatrains and a couplet), elegies, and lyrics such as 'The soote season', 'Alas, so all things now do hold their peace', and the elegy on Wyatt — printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
plot_or_argument: A courtier's lyric record: love's complaints, the seasons' changes, the deaths of friends, and the poet's imprisonment at Windsor, all in a grave, musical decasyllabic line.
narrative_structure: Miscellany of sonnets and lyrics without narrative frame; Tottel's printed canon of forty poems is the principal witness.
principal_characters: the speaker; the beloved ('Geraldine', Elizabeth Fitzgerald); the court
meter_and_prosody: The regular iambic pentameter and the English sonnet rhyme scheme (abab cdcd efef gg) that Surrey perfected and Shakespeare inherited; smooth alternation of the accents.
historical_context: Written in the last decade of Surrey's life, under the factional warfare that ended in his execution in 1547; the elegy on Wyatt makes the dead poet a mirror of his own fate.
literary_significance: With Wyatt, the founder of the English sonnet; Surrey's smoother line and his rhyme scheme became the Elizabethan standard, and Tottel's printing of his verse made him the model of the English courtly poet.
attribution_notes: The Tottel canon of forty poems is accepted in the main; a few attributions are contested.
bibliographical_notes: Tottel's Miscellany (1557). Standard edition: Emrys Jones (ed.), Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey: Poems (Clarendon Press, 1964).

title: Aeneid, Books II and IV (Surrey's translation)
description: Surrey's translation of Virgil's Aeneid, Books II and IV — the fall of Troy and the tragedy of Dido — in unrhymed iambic pentameter, the first English blank verse. Book IV was printed by John Day in 1554 and both books in Tottel's 1557 edition; the translation fixed the metre that Marlowe and Shakespeare made the language of English drama.
plot_or_argument: Book II: Aeneas recounts Troy's last night — the horse, the burning, Priam's death, the loss of Creusa. Book IV: Dido's passion for Aeneas, their union in the cave, his departure, and her suicide on the pyre.
narrative_structure: Two books of the epic, chosen for their pathos; the translation follows Virgil book by book without prologue apparatus.
principal_characters: Aeneas; Dido; Priam; Sinon; Anna; Mercury
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter — used for the first time in English; the line Surrey invented from the Italian versi sciolti and Virgil's hexameter.
historical_context: Translated in Surrey's last years, when he stood near the throne; the fall of Troy and the ruin of Dido's court read as parables of Henrician politics.
literary_significance: The invention of blank verse, the metre of English tragedy and epic from Marlowe to Milton; alongside Douglas's Scots Eneados, the founding translation of Virgil into English.
bibliographical_notes: Book IV printed by John Day, 1554; Books II and IV in Tottel's Miscellany (1557). Standard edition: Frederick Morgan Padelford (ed.), The Poems of Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey (University of Washington Press, 1928).

title: The Pastime of Pleasure
alternative_titles: The Historie of Graunde Amoure and La Bell Pucell
description: Hawes's allegorical romance of the education of the knight Graunde Amoure: his instruction by Lady Fame and the seven liberal arts in the Tower of Doctrine, his courtship of La Belle Pucelle, his combat with a giant, their marriage, and his death, with Time and Eternity closing the poem. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1509, it is the last great allegory of the medieval English tradition.
plot_or_argument: Graunde Amoure, guided by Governance and instructed in the Tower of Doctrine, wins La Belle Pucelle through the arts and arms, marries her, and rules until Age and Death take him; Fame memorializes the lovers.
narrative_structure: An allegorical romance in three movements — instruction, quest, and the fall of the hero — framed by a dream prologue and an epilogue on fame and time.
principal_characters: Graunde Amoure; La Belle Pucelle; Lady Fame; Governance; Godfrey Gobelive (the giant); Time; Eternity
literary_form: allegorical romance in rhyme royal and couplets
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal handled in the Lydgatian manner, with couplet passages; aureate diction over a clear narrative line.
historical_context: Written at the court of Henry VII, to whom the ideal of the educated knight was addressed; printed in 1509, the year of Henry VIII's accession.
literary_significance: The bridge between the medieval allegorical romance and Tudor poetry; its catalogue of the arts and its ideal of the learned knight were formative for Spenser's Faerie Queene.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Wynkyn de Worde, 1509. Standard edition: William Edward Mead (ed.), The Pastime of Pleasure (EETS, 1928).

title: The Example of Virtue
description: Hawes's first major poem, an allegory of the soul's life: Youth, guided by Discretion, journeys through the world and learns virtue's lessons from Lady Sapience, marries Cleanness, and passes through Age to the vision of Eternity. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1504.
plot_or_argument: Youth, counselled by Discretion, crosses the sea of the world, defeats the dragon of vice, and is led by Sapience and Fortune's lessons to the marriage with Cleanness; Age overtakes him, and the soul enters Eternity.
narrative_structure: A moral allegory in the pilgrimage form, moving from instruction through trial to the vision of eternity.
principal_characters: Youth; Discretion; Lady Sapience; Cleanness; Fortune; Age; Eternity
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal in the Lydgatian manner, with aureate vocabulary.
historical_context: Written early in the reign of Henry VII, when the court still sustained the allegorical tradition of the fifteenth century.
literary_significance: A minor but characteristic example of the late medieval moral allegory, showing the tradition Spenser was to transform.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Wynkyn de Worde, c. 1504. Standard edition: Mead (1928) reprints portions; full text in F. J. Furnivall's edition (EETS, 1864).

title: The Ship of Fools
alternative_titles: The Shyp of Folys of the Worlde
description: Barclay's Englishing of Sebastian Brant's Narrenschiff through Locher's Latin version: a fleet of fools — the bookish fool, the covetous, the gluttonous, the lecherous clergy, the negligent bishops — each shipped aboard the vessel of folly in a comprehensive satire of the estates, printed by Richard Pynson in 1509.
plot_or_argument: The narrator gathers the fools of every estate aboard the Ship of Fools; chapter by chapter, each folly is exhibited and moralized, from the pride of scholars to the corruption of Rome.
narrative_structure: A catalogue satire in over a hundred sections, each an emblem of a folly with its moral appended; the ship provides the unifying frame.
principal_characters: the narrator; the fools (by estate and vice)
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas of fluent competence; the moralized catalogue form of the continental Renaissance satire.
historical_context: Translated in the years before the Reformation, when anticlerical satire was already a licensed genre; printed by Pynson in December 1509.
literary_significance: The channel by which the great European estates satire reached England; its catalogue form and its moralizing woodcuts shaped a century of English satirical writing.
attribution_notes: Barclay's adaptation of Brant (via Locher) is freely made with English additions; recorded as translation-adaptation.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Pynson, 1509. Standard edition: T. H. Jamieson (ed.), The Ship of Fools (Edinburgh, 1874).

title: The Eclogues (Barclay)
description: Barclay's five eclogues, the first English pastoral poetry: three adapted from Mantuan and two from Aeneas Sylvius's De Curialium Miseriis, in which shepherds debate the miseries of courts and the corruption of the clergy, and the city's poverty is set against the country's sufficiency.
plot_or_argument: Shepherds — Coridon, Cornix, Faustus, Amyntas — meet and debate in turn: the woes of courtiers, the pride of churchmen, the pleasures of the country life, and the duties of the rich toward the poor.
narrative_structure: Five discrete eclogues in the Virgilian-Mantuan manner, each a debate between named shepherds with its moral explicit.
principal_characters: Coridon; Cornix; Faustus; Amyntas; Codrus; Minalcas
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal for the pastoral dialogue; the smooth didactic verse of the early Tudor humanists.
historical_context: Written in the decade when the court satire was becoming the period's dominant mode; the eclogues import the Mantuan model that every Elizabethan grammar school would memorize.
literary_significance: The first English pastoral, founding the tradition that runs through Spenser's Shepheardes Calender to the great pastoral of the 1590s.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the eclogues are adaptations of Mantuan and Aeneas Sylvius.
bibliographical_notes: Eclogues I–III printed c. 1518, IV–V c. 1521; collected in The Certayne Egloges (1570). Standard edition: Beatrice White (ed.), The Eclogues of Alexander Barclay (EETS, 1928).

title: The Palice of Honour
description: Douglas's first major poem, a courtly dream vision of prodigious learning: the dreamer, in a wilderness, sees a procession of the courts of Venus, Diana, and Minerva, faints before Venus's pageant, and is led to the Palace of Honour, where he learns the true source of fame and virtue. An answer to Chaucer's House of Fame and the foundation of Douglas's poetic career.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer journeys with a guide from the garden of desire through the courts of Venus and Diana to the Palace of Honour, where the great of all ages sit enthroned; waking, he commits himself to the pursuit of honour through virtue.
narrative_structure: A dream vision in three movements — desire, instruction, and the vision of honour — modelled on Chaucer's House of Fame.
principal_characters: the dreamer; Venus; Diana; Minerva; Calliope (guide)
meter_and_prosody: The nine-line stanza (ababbcbcC) inherited from Chaucer; aureate diction and encyclopaedic allusion.
historical_context: Written about 1501, when Douglas was provost of St Giles; the poem's learning advertises the Scottish court's claim to the European Renaissance.
literary_significance: The most learned poem of the Scottish Renaissance and a central text of the Chaucerians; its allegorical courts prefigure The Faerie Queene.
bibliographical_notes: Printed c. 1553 (London, William Copland). Standard edition: Priscilla Bawcutt (ed.), The Shorter Poems of Gavin Douglas (Scottish Text Society, 1967).

title: King Hart
description: Douglas's allegory of the life of man: King Hart rules his castle of the body with the five senses as his servants until Dame Pleasance and her court — Youthheid, Fresche Delyte, Wantonness — enter and corrupt him; age, sickness, and death storm the castle, and the soul departs. The great Scots allegory of the body politic and the body natural.
plot_or_argument: King Hart, counselled by Ressoun, admits Dame Pleasance and her court; the castle falls into riot; Conscience, Ressoun, and Wisdome are driven out; Age besieges and takes the castle, and Hart dies, leaving his soul to God's judgement.
narrative_structure: A sustained allegory of the besieged castle in the morality tradition, moving from the entrance of pleasure through riot to death and judgement.
principal_characters: King Hart; Dame Pleasance; Youthheid; Fresche Delyte; Ressoun; Conscience; Age; Decrepitness
meter_and_prosody: Stanzaic verse in the Chaucerian tradition; vigorous personification allegory.
historical_context: Written in Douglas's maturity, perhaps after the death of James IV at Flodden (1513); the castle's fall shadows the fall of the king's court.
literary_significance: The finest Scots allegory of the body's rule and a bridge between the moralities and the Renaissance anatomy of the self; admired by the later Scots poets.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Douglas on manuscript authority; the attribution is generally accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Single MS witness (c. 1560s); first printed 1786 (Pinkerton). Standard edition: Bawcutt (1967).

title: Eneados
description: Douglas's complete translation of Virgil's Aeneid into Scots couplets, completed on 22 July 1513 — the first full translation of the poem in any British language — with a thirteenth book from Mapheus Vegius, and a prologue to each book in which the translator speaks of the Scottish seasons, his art, and his critics. Printed at London in 1553.
plot_or_argument: Virgil's epic entire: Aeneas's flight from Troy, the wanderings, the tragedy of Dido, the descent to the underworld, and the wars in Italy — with Vegius's supplement completing the hero's apotheosis.
narrative_structure: Twelve books of the Aeneid plus the thirteenth book of Vegius; each book preceded by a prologue, of which the seasonal prologues (VII, XII, XIII) are the most celebrated.
principal_characters: Aeneas; Dido; Turnus; Anchises; Venus; Juno
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets in vigorous Scots; the prologues alternate aureate and plain registers with seasonal description.
historical_context: Completed in the year of Flodden (1513), when the Scottish court and much of its nobility were destroyed; Douglas's translation of the epic of exile and foundation speaks to a nation in crisis.
literary_significance: The first complete British Aeneid and the summit of Scots humanist translation; its prologues are the finest nature poetry in Scots, and the translation passed Virgil to the northern Renaissance.
bibliographical_notes: Printed 1553 (London, William Copland). Standard edition: David F. C. Coldwell (ed.), Virgil's Aeneid Translated into Scottish Verse by Gavin Douglas (Scottish Text Society, 4 vols, 1957–64).

title: The Dreme
alternative_titles: The Dreme of Schir David Lindsay
description: Lindsay's dream vision addressed to the young James V: the poet, transported in sleep to hell, purgatory, and paradise, meets the spirit of the king's ancestors and returns to instruct the king in the duties of rule — an epistle to the sovereign that founds Lindsay's career as the conscience of the Scottish crown.
plot_or_argument: The poet dreams he travels with Dame Remembrance through the three realms, hears the lament of the dead Scots kings over the realm's decay, and wakes to write the 'Exhortation to the King' that closes the poem.
narrative_structure: Dream vision with epilogue; the three-realm journey frames the political exhortation, which is the poem's true centre.
principal_characters: the poet; Dame Remembrance; James V (addressed); the dead kings
literary_form: dream vision in couplets and stanzas
meter_and_prosody: Scots couplets and stanzaic passages in the Makar tradition; plain, forceful didactic verse.
historical_context: Written in 1528 as James V escaped the Douglas faction and took personal rule; Lindsay, his childhood companion, speaks as the king's tutor and conscience.
literary_significance: The classic Scots poem of princely counsel and the seed of the Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis; its vision of national decay set the tone of the Scottish Reformation's literature.
bibliographical_notes: Composed 1528; printed in the sixteenth-century collected editions of Lindsay's works. Standard edition: Douglas Hamer (ed.), The Works of Sir David Lindsay (Scottish Text Society, 1931–36).

title: The Testament of the Papyngo
alternative_titles: The Testament and Complaynt of Our Soverane Lordis Papyngo
description: Lindsay's satire of court and church: the king's parrot, dying after a fall from the palace wall, makes her testament — leaving her heart to the king, her body to the courtiers, and her counsel to the clergy — and delivers a dying bird's-eye satire of the bishops, the court, and the vices of the age.
plot_or_argument: The Papyngo, perched high on the palace wall, falls and dies; before death she disposes of her estate in a testament that satirizes each legatee in turn, closing with an epistle to the bishops on their duties.
narrative_structure: The testament form — the dying bird's will and last counsel — used as a vehicle for estates satire; mock-legal framework, satirical legacies, and a closing sermon.
principal_characters: the Papyngo; James V (legatee); the courtiers; the bishops
literary_form: verse satire in the testament tradition
meter_and_prosody: Scots couplets and stanzas; the mock-legal diction of the testament handled with satirical point.
historical_context: Written in 1530 as the Scottish church's wealth and the court's corruption became the subjects of Reformation debate; the parrot speaks with the licence of the dying.
literary_significance: The wittiest of Lindsay's satires and a classic of the Scots complaint; its parrot looks back to Skelton's Speke Parrot and forward to the beast satires of the later century.
bibliographical_notes: Composed 1530; printed in the sixteenth-century collected editions. Standard edition: Hamer (1931–36).

title: Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis
alternative_titles: The Satire of the Three Estates
description: Lindsay's great morality drama of the Scottish Reformation: King Humanitie, seduced by Sensualitie and the vices, is recalled to virtue by Divine Correction, and summons a parliament of the three estates — Spirituality, Temporalitie, Merchant — where John the Common-Weill indicts the church's abuses and the vices are tried and hanged. Played at Linlithgow in 1540 and enlarged at Cupar in 1552.
plot_or_argument: Rex Humanitas falls under the rule of Wantonness, Placebo, and Solace; Divine Correction reforms him; the estates meet in parliament, hear John the Common-Weill's complaint, and pass the acts of reform, the play closing with the sermon of Folly.
narrative_structure: A two-part morality expanded to a national parliament: the king's moral fall and recovery (Part I) and the public trial and reformation of the estates (Part II).
principal_characters: Rex Humanitas; Divine Correction; Sensualitie; Flatterie; Falset; Dissait; John the Common-Weill; Spirituality; Temporalitie; Merchant
meter_and_prosody: Scots couplets of great stage energy; songs, interludes, and the sermon of Folly closing the action.
historical_context: First played before James V at Linlithgow in 1540; the enlarged Cupar performance (1552) addressed the eve of the Scottish Reformation, and the play remained in performance for a century.
literary_significance: The greatest Scottish play and the dramatic summa of the northern Reformation; its parliament scene made drama an instrument of national reform and remained a living text into the seventeenth century.
bibliographical_notes: Printed 1602 (Edinburgh, Robert Charteris). Standard edition: Roderick Lyall (ed.), Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis (Canongate, 1989).

title: Tottel's Miscellany
alternative_titles: Songes and Sonettes, written by the ryght honorable Lorde Henry Haward late Earle of Surrey, and other
description: The first great printed anthology of English poetry: 271 poems by Surrey, Wyatt, Nicholas Grimald, and other courtly poets, published by Richard Tottel on 5 June 1557 under the title Songes and Sonettes. It fixed the public canon of the Henrician lyric and went through nine editions by 1587.
plot_or_argument: An anthology without narrative frame: sonnets, songs, elegies, and epigrams arranged by author, beginning with Surrey, whose name gave the volume its selling title.
narrative_structure: Miscellany organized by poet, with the Earl of Surrey's poems first; the arrangement itself constitutes the first printed history of the English lyric.
principal_characters: the courtly poets (Surrey, Wyatt, Grimald, and others)
literary_form: anthology of sonnets, lyrics, and epigrams
meter_and_prosody: The full range of the early Tudor lyric: sonnets, poulter's measure, short-line songs; the anthology standardized the decasyllabic line for a public audience.
historical_context: Printed two years after the Marian restoration began; the miscellany carried the Henrician court's poetry into the Elizabethan age and made the court lyric a national possession.
literary_significance: The founding anthology of English poetry: it created the reading public for the lyric, fixed the reputations of Wyatt and Surrey, and supplied the Elizabethan poets with their metre and manner.
attribution_notes: Compiled by Richard Tottel (publisher); the authorship of the 'uncertain authors' poems remains largely unknown. Recorded as collaborative with no author links, per the validator's anonymity rule.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Tottel, 1557 (nine editions by 1587). Standard edition: Amanda Holton and Tom MacFaul (eds.), Tottel's Miscellany (Penguin, 2011).
